title: The 5 Biggest Stars We Know, Ranked (#1 Isn't in Our Galaxy)

scenes.text: The five biggest stars we know of. Number one isn't even in our galaxy.
Number five: Mu Cephei, the Garnet Star. About 1,260 times the Sun's radius. The biggest star you can see with your own eyes.
scenes.label: Mu Cephei · ~1,260 Suns

scenes.text: Number four: AH Scorpii. About 1,400 Suns across, measured directly with an array of telescopes, and astronomers still argue over it.
scenes.label: AH Scorpii · ~1,400 Suns

scenes.text: Number three: VY Canis Majoris, 3,900 light years away. About 1,420 Suns. Put it where our Sun is and it swallows Jupiter.
scenes.label: VY Canis Majoris · ~1,420

scenes.text: Number two: RSGC1-F01, hidden in dust 22,000 light years away. About 1,530 Suns, and visible only in infrared.
scenes.label: RSGC1-F01 · ~1,530 Suns

scenes.text: Number one: WOH G64, in the Large Magellanic Cloud, 160,000 light years away. About 1,540 Suns. In 2024 we photographed it: the first close-up of a star outside the Milky Way.
scenes.label: WOH G64 · ~1,540 Suns

description:
The five largest known stars, ranked by estimated radius in Suns.
All five are red supergiants, each so wide that in the Sun's place its surface would reach past Jupiter's orbit. Number one, WOH G64, lies in a neighbouring galaxy, the Large Magellanic Cloud, and in 2024 the European Southern Observatory took the first close-up image of it. These sizes are estimates with large error bars and get revised as distances improve; the often-quoted Stephenson 2-18, at around 2,150 Suns, is disputed and left off this list.
Which of these giants would you most want to see up close, and what should we rank next?
first_comment: Which would you put at number one? UY Scuti used to top these lists at 1,700 Suns, until better distance data shrank it to about 900. What should we rank next?
